newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe gold producers may seek local floor price.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe gold producers may seek local floor price.

text.p: Zimbabwe gold producers may seek a guaranteed local gold floor price to improve their viability which is threatened by low world gold prices and rising input costs, a top industry official said on Wednesday.
Derek Bain, chief executive of the Zimbabwe Chamber of Mines, told Reuters that some gold companies may be forced to retrench workers in coming months as part of efforts to stay viable.

"The low prices and rising input costs are driving some producers to the wall...and we are discussing these and other problems," he said on the eve of a two-day annual general congress of the chamber of mines.

The conference, set for the northern resort town of Victoria Falls, will focus on Zimbabwe's mining sector in general and in the southern African region, but Bain said the subject of a fixed gold floor price may be a major topic on the sidelines.

"We have sounded out the (central) Reserve Bank on the matter...and we are soon going to present a paper to the bank. We are still getting information from various mines and as soon as we finish our compilation, we will forward the paper to the central bank," he said.
Under the scheme, the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe which currently markets the local gold, would pay producers guaranteed prices irrespective of the movement of the world price.
"This will cushion producers, especially the smaller mines, from fluctuations of the gold price being currently experienced," he said, emphasising the discussions were at an initial stage.
Bain said the gold mining sector -- Zimbabwe's second largest export earner after tobacco -- was also worried rising costs are squeezing profit margins.

Last month, the president of the Zimbabwe Chamber of Mines, Roy Pitchford warned companies to look out for a possible rise in power tariffs and prepare for annual wage increases, which unions want to climb above 27 percent in the financial year starting in July from last year's 25 percent.
Input costs have risen steadily over the years, averaging 32 percent annually in the last three years, according to state statistics.
"Outside these two negatives -- low prices and input costs -- the (gold) industry looks fairly solid and promising," Bain said, citing an increase in gold exploration over the last seven years.

Zimbabwe, Africa's third largest gold producer after South Africa and Ghana, last year mined 24.7 tonnes of gold valued at Z$3.04 billion (U.S$270 million), a slight increase over the 24.3 tonnes mined in 1995, and down on the projected 26 tonnes.
Industry analysts say many local companies scaled down production in late 1996 when the gold price fell to a record low of U.S.$330 per ounce.
The price is expected to hover around $345-365 in the next six months.

The southern African state's leading gold producers include Falcon Gold, which shed nearly 200 workers at its Dalny mine in March citing viability problems, Rio Tinto, Lonrho Zimbabwe and Ashanti Goldfields Zimbabwe.
